articles.title: Austin Smotherman's Bank of Utah Championship win was a story 10 years in the making
articles.summary: In his 100th career PGA Tour start, Austin Smotherman finally achieved a lifelong dream in Utah.
articles.body:
Back in March, Austin Smotherman entered Sunday at the Cognizant Championship on the precipice of his dream. Holding the 54-hole lead in a PGA Tour event for the first time in his career, the then-31-year-old faced the most terrifying round of his career. He navigated PGA National well enough that Sunday, but finished T2 as Nico Echavarria claimed the title after Shane Lowry imploded. But after he tapped in to close out his day, Smotherman looked like a man who had just won .

Because he knew that was a necessary step to get to where he eventually wanted to go.

"This was kind of just my first really big pedestal," Smotherman said that Sunday. "Kind of had a back door-ish top 5 in the Mexico Open at Vidanta a couple years ago, and never really had the same kind of moments coming down the stretch … This will be a week I always look back at."

That got Smotherman into his first-career Signature Event at the Arnold Palmer Invitational. He withdrew from Bay Hill with an injury but posted a T13 at the Players the next week. But the breakthrough never came, as the rest of Smotherman's season was filled with missed cuts and mediocre finishes. He finished 80th in the FedEx Cup standings and missed the playoffs, but the feeling that he was close remained.

That led him to this week at the Bank of Utah Championship , his 100th career PGA Tour start, where everything finally clicked.

He opened with a 63 at Black Desert Resort and followed it up with a 62 to take the lead into the weekend. A Saturday 6-under 65 gave him his second-career 54-hole lead and another chance at the hardest thing in professional golf: closing out your first win.

"It would be just a lifelong dream come true," Smotherman said on Saturday about the possibility of getting the job done.

But achieving your dreams is never an easy task. It's a frightening prospect that can turn your legs to jelly and numb your hands. Being so close to the one thing you've always wanted, the thing you've worked your entire life to achieve, can be paralyzing.

Austin Smotherman knew what awaited him because he faced it in March at PGA National.

He started Sunday's final round with a one-shot lead over Doug Ghim but quickly calmed his nerves with birdies at 1, 4 and 5 to stretch his lead. Smotherman then made seven straight pars before reality set in, and the final stretch to his dreams started to lengthen as the nerves tightened. He found the fairway on the par-4 13th but lost his second shot into the lip of a greenside bunker. His third shot went just 24 feet and landed in another greenside bunker. He eventually made double bogey, and his lead shrank from three to one.

But Smotherman knew there were gettable holes ahead. He bounced back with a birdie on the drivable par-4 14th and another on 16. A bogey at 17 shrunk his lead over Ghim to two, but once Smotherman found the fairway at the par-5 18th, he knew he had finally made it.

His second shot landed just short of the green, allowing him to two-putt for birdie to finish at 26 under and claim his first PGA Tour title. When Smotherman knocked in his final putt, he hugged his caddie and Ghim before embracing his wife on the green. Then, when Austin Smotherman was asked to put everything into words, the emotions started to flow—the emotions of a 10-year journey that saw him spend two years on PGA Tour Latin America, two-plus on the Korn Ferry Tour and 100 starts on the PGA Tour before finally becoming a champion.

"Oh my gosh," a bleary-eyed Smotherman told Golf Channel's Amy Rogers after his win. "Just hit it just good enough [today], hit it close early to take some pressure off. … Oh my gosh, we won on the PGA Tour. That's insane.

"Gosh … we did it! Let's go!" Smotherman yelled as his interview ended.

An hour later, with the trophy beside him, the PGA Tour's newest champion looked back on the long road he traveled from SMU to the moment that occurred Sunday in Utah. He talked about the "learning curves" he faced at each level of professional golf and how this moment could lead to even more. But talk of the next 100 starts or a next title can wait. For Austin Smotherman, Sunday was all about how far he'd come, what he learned and how he finally turned long-shot golf dreams into reality.

"One hundred starts out here is an incredible number, just to have 100 starts," Smotherman said. "But even more so, to play professional golf now for 10 years, travel the world, have the support I've had, it's pretty unreal to lift a trophy at the highest level. It's something we've dreamed about since I was a kid. Here we are."

Ten years and a lot of professional scars later, Austin Smotherman finally reached his destination because he always believed he'd get there. Some dreams just take time.

articles.title: Korn Ferry Tour: Sandy Scott breaks into top 100 with back-to-back wins after career-threatening injury
articles.summary: Scottish golfer Sandy Scott secured his second-straight victory on the Korn Ferry Tour on Sunday to move to the top of the US circuit's Points List; watch the PGA Tour's Baycurrent Classic in Yokohama, Japan, live on Sky Sports Golf from 4am on Thursday
articles.body:
The 28-year-old from Nairn defeated William Sides in a four-hole play-off at The Patriot Golf Club to shoot to the top of the US circuit's Points List, heading into next week's Korn Ferry Tour Championship.

It comes just two weeks after he secured his first victory on the PGA Tour feeder circuit at the Nationwide Children's Hospital Championship, a win which earned Scott a PGA Tour card for the 2027 season.

Scott has now broken into the world's top 100, with this weekend's triumph in Oklahoma lifting him to 87th in the Official World Golf Ranking.

Seven years ago, the former Walker Cup player was preparing to turn professional when a serious wrist injury left him fearing he might never play competitive golf again.

Scott tore the ligaments in his right wrist and underwent two surgeries in 2019, forcing him to spend around 24 months on the sidelines.

"I have always had the belief that I can do it," he said. "That's why we all tee it up. I think that's where we all see ourselves going.

"Belief is a big part of this game. Doing it this way is pretty special."

After recovering from surgery, Scott spent two years grinding his way through PGA Tour Latinoamerica and PGA Tour Americas, eventually earning his place on the Korn Ferry Tour after finishing eighth in the latter's Order of Merit in 2024.

"I'm proud of the fight to get here," he added. "I'm grateful for the support that I've had. Looking back on those times is pretty neat."

The wrist injury continues to cause him some discomfort, with Scott sidelined for another two months earlier in the 2026 season.

"I have gone through some ups and downs, injuries and whatnot," said the Texas Tech alumnus.

"When it first flared up in college, it took a couple of surgeries and some steroid injections, and I was out for the best part of two years."

"It took a lot of perseverance and help. A couple of months ago it flared up, but I did the right things.

"I let it heal and came back feeling good. I think it'll just be a case of management.

"I know what helps it and hurts it now, but I feel good now."

Scott began Sunday's final round three shots behind 54-hole leader Trent Phillips, but a six-under 64 sent him surging up the leaderboard and into a tie with Sides after 72 holes.

Neither player could be separated through the first three play-off holes, but Scott finally gained the advantage at the fourth when Sides found a greenside bunker with his approach.

The British golfer landed his ball on the green and holed out for birdie.

"I was pretty delighted when the putt went in," Scott, who now has two wins and a runner-up finish in his last three starts, said.

"There was probably some relief there as well. It was a long day."

Scott will now hope to cap off 2026 as the tour's season-long points race leader, with a strong finish at next week's Korn Ferry Tour Championship.

"I came into this week with a blank slate in my mind," he added.

"I'm trying to do the same stuff, play the same golf, commit to the shots.

"In the conversations my caddie and I have had, we tried to be as consistent as possible. I'm just going to take that into next week and see where we end up."

articles.body:
Sandy Scott has moved into the world's top 100 at 87th after winning for the second week in a row on the Korn Ferry Tour.

He is top of the second-tier Korn Ferry Tour points list and has obtained PGA Tour membership for 2027.

articles.title: Tiger Woods is helping open a $2.5 billion, 914-acre Texas golf community with 500 planned homes, an 18-hole course, dude ranch and resort-style amenities; residential prices start at $1 million
articles.summary: Tiger Woods is helping launch a new gated golf community outside Fort Worth, Texas, where homes will start at $1 million.
articles.body: Tiger Woods is helping launch a new gated golf community outside Fort Worth, Texas, where homes will start at $1 million. As per Realtor, Bluejack Ranch spread accross 914-acre, is planned as a $2.5 billion community with 500 custom and semi-custom homes, an 18-hole golf course and a range of resort-style facilities.The community is located in Aledo, about a 20-minute drive from downtown Fort Worth. It is the second Bluejack golf community created through a partnership involving Woods, developer Andy Mitchell and professional golfer J J Henry. The first, Bluejack National, is in Montgomery, Texas, about three hours away.Bluejack Ranch is expected to open this autumn. Its planned homes will vary widely in size, from 1,282-square-foot two-bedroom casitas to large estate homes. Estate properties will sit on sites of up to one acre and will have at least 4,000 square feet of living space. Some larger houses are expected to exceed 19,000 square feet and could cost tens of millions of dollars.While residential properties will start at $1 million, buyers can also purchase half-acre lots starting at $775,000 and build on them. All lot buyers will have to use a Bluejack builder. The average home is expected to cost between $2 million and $4 million.A golf community designed around familiesThe development is being built around more than golf. Its plans include a private golf club, a working dude ranch, an entertainment hall, podcast studios, multiple pools, tennis and pickleball courts, a bowling alley, restaurants, a spa and wellness centre, and a recreation centre for all ages. The community will also have 24/7 gated security.The golf facilities are being designed by Woods' TGR Design in collaboration with land planner Beau Welling. There will be a championship 18-hole course, a 10-hole short course and a practice facility with a driving range and three putting greens.The main course will stretch almost 8,000 yards from the longest "Tiger tees". It has been grassed with Stadium Zoysia. Together, the golf courses will cover about 135 acres.Developer Andy Mitchell said the aim was to make the community useful for people who may not play golf. "You live on 900 acres with every form of entertainment imaginable," Mitchell told Realtor.com. "You don't need a big home, necessarily. It's like going to a resort, you don't have to build your own game room."The project is also expected to have a commercial area near the front "greeter's barn". Mitchell said it is intended to include "high-end lifestyle brands" that fit the community's "laidback luxury" theme.Woods and Mitchell's partnershipMitchell first met Woods in 2013. At the time, Woods was starting his golf-course design business. A mutual friend introduced the two, leading to a collaboration that became Bluejack National, Woods' first US golf-course design project.Mitchell said the two have remained close through their work together. "We're both fathers, our kids are similar age," he said. "We're literally one month apart. We're a lot alike. We both love to win. I can't hide it, he can't hide it." He added, "If we're going to do something, he wants it to be the best."The partnership on Bluejack Ranch also includes Henry. Mitchell said the second community was not something he had originally planned. "It wasn't like I was looking to do another course," he said. "It just organically happened."For Mitchell, the project is also connected to his interest in golf and family activities. He said the development is not simply a golf project, but a real estate venture built around families across generations. "I love Tiger and I love golf," he said. "But this real estate play is about multigenerational family club."That focus can also be seen in the facilities being planned for residents who do not play golf. Mitchell said his wife and business partner, Kristin, had a major say in features intended to appeal to everyone from grandparents to grandchildren.Ranch life alongside golfOne of the unusual parts of Bluejack Ranch will be its dude ranch. It is planned to have 10 horses, miniature Highland cows, donkeys, a Labrador retriever and a small herd of longhorn cattle.Mitchell said the development initially bought three longhorns, but two were pregnant. The cattle are "protected", he said, and will not be used as food.The ranch will be open to both experienced riders and beginners who need lessons. Staff will take care of the animals, while residents can spend time around them.Mitchell said ranch workers even joked about the quality of the animal facilities. "They'd say, 'Hey, Andy, nice horse mansion,'" he said.Mitchell also pointed to the different interests of Woods' children while explaining the idea behind the community. Woods' daughter, Sam Alexis, is studying at Stanford University and is focused on premed courses, while his son, Charlie, is pursuing golf. "She might want to bring her friends out, sit at the spa, do yoga, hang out and run and jog," Mitchell said.Costs extend beyond the homesThe price of buying into Bluejack Ranch goes beyond the cost of a home or lot. Monthly homeowners' association fees will run into the thousands of dollars, helping pay for the upkeep of the community's shared areas and amenities.The private golf club also has separate costs. One-time initiation fees can reach $225,000, while monthly dues can be around $3,000, depending on the membership tier and level of golf access.However, buying a home does not automatically guarantee club membership. Prospective members still have to be invited and vetted.Mitchell said this was intended to protect the private club even if a homeowner later sells their property. "I can't control who you sell your home to," he said. "The way I protect the club is if you sell your home to somebody who should not be in the club- imagine the biggest villain you know- he will never get into the club."Despite the high costs, Mitchell said the project is ultimately meant to offer a place where residents can step away from their usual routines. He also wants Woods to be able to spend time there without being constantly approached by fans."You're free to be Tiger Woods," Mitchell said. "Nobody is going to solicit you or ask for your autograph." He said the larger idea behind Bluejack Ranch is not only luxury or golf, but time with family and friends. "Bluejack is, 'Why don't you unplug?'" Mitchell said. "Come on out, turn your phone off, go hang out with cattle, be close to nature." He added, "I love it when members get here and say, 'Andy, I need a little more Bluejack.'"Ready to Make a Smarter Property Decision? Build Your Legacy with TOI Homes.

articles.title: Jewish Greens chair says she could leave party over 'Zionism is racism' motion
articles.summary: The motion, which has divided senior party figures, backs a "single democratic Palestinian state in all of historic Palestine".
articles.body:
The chair of Jewish Greens Vivien Lichtenstein has told the BBC it is "quite possible" she will leave the party after Green members adopted a motion declaring Zionism a form of racism.

The motion, which has divided senior party figures, also backs a "single democratic Palestinian state in all of historic Palestine", which includes modern-day Israel.

It has been condemned by some Jewish groups and Israel's foreign ministry.

Asked by BBC Radio 4's Today programme about her future, Lichtenstein said: "I haven't decided yet...It is quite possible that I will leave the party...I'm giving it a little time and to talk with colleagues."

Lichtenstein, who is a former chair of her local party, said she had opposed the motion from the first time she heard about it.

"I don't think it's helpful and it doesn't make any difference whatsoever to Palestinians in Gaza who have suffered devastation, orphans left behind, it doesn't make any difference to Palestinians in the West Bank who are currently suffering, are currently being attacked and killed."

Members of the Green Party of England and Wales endorsed the policy motion, which was put forward by a group of activists at the party's conference in Brighton, by 1,022 votes to 813.

There are 230,000 members of the Green party overall and not everyone attended the conference.

The party's leader Zack Polanski, who is himself Jewish, had called for the motion to be amended to add in protections for Jewish members and remove language referring to a "single democratic Palestinian State". Both of these amendments were defeated.

Polanski did not stay at conference to vote on either this or the substantive motion. He left early to campaign in Holborn and St Pancras, where he is standing in a by-election to be the MP. A full list of candidates in the contest can be found here .

The motion, among other statements, "supports the establishment of a single democratic Palestinian State in all of historic Palestine with Jerusalem as its capital, equal rights for all, and the right of return for Palestinians and their descendants".

It defines Zionism as an ideology supporting "an ethnonationalist Jewish state".

The Board of Deputies of British Jews and the Jewish Leadership Council, which criticised the motion, said "Zionism is anti-racism, creating a refuge for Jews in their ancient homeland after millennia of persecution outside it".

Lichtenstein said she defines herself as "both Zionist and anti-Zionist" depending on the definition, and said a problem with the motion is that there are many definitions.

She said she was not concerned about "people accusing me of supporting Israel's right to exist and therefore I'm a racist, which of course is not the case", but said the "very bad motion...crosses a line".

One way in which it did that, she said, was that the proposers said they had consulted some Jews, but did not consult the Jewish Greens, who would have made some amendments to improve the motion.

She said there was a "vast range" of opinions among Jewish Greens, some who supported the motion entirely, others who supported aspects, and others who were against it. Some Jewish Greens also support one state, she added.

She said that party policy was that "it's up to Israelis and Palestinians to choose their future - one state or two".

Last month, the UK and 11 allies reiterated their support for a two-state solution , which would recognise a Palestinian state alongside an Israeli one. Israel rejects a two-state solution.

Her concern with the motion was that the Green Party may accuse UK, Israeli, or Jewish organisations, including those that partner with Palestinians, of racism. She said she supports many of these groups working "against the occupation and even go out on the ground to assist Palestinians".

She said she knows of some non-Jews who are planning on not staying in the party because "they think the motion crosses a line" and also because of their work, if they might not be able to be associated with a party that has "Zionism is racism" as a policy.

Asked whether she believed there were antisemites inside the party, including at senior levels, she said "there are certainly some antisemites in the party, I don't know about at senior level, that is not my experience".

In response to the motion, Israel's foreign ministry said it had banned Polanski from entering the country.

A Green spokeswoman insisted the party would protect Jewish members - and they would not be persecuted for attending synagogues which defined themselves as Zionist.

Speaking after the vote, Lubna Speitan, the Green member behind the motion, argued its backers wanted to voice opposition to "racist systems of oppression".

"We stand united against all forms of racism and discrimination - no exemptions," she added.

Four of the party's five MPs - Ellie Chowns, Adrian Ramsay, Carla Denyer, and Sian Berry - had publicly opposed it, but the leadership was divided.

In her interview on the Today programme on Friday, co-deputy leader Rachel Millward had called the motion "problematic", while her counterpart Mothin Ali told the BBC on Saturday he would support the motion in its original form.

The Movement for Progressive Judaism, one of the largest and most liberal strands of Judaism in the UK, released a statement condemning the motion, which it said was "antisemitic in its formulation and intention".

"Jewish self-determination is a right. Declaring it racist is an attack on Jews," the statement read.

Chief Rabbi Sir Ephraim Mirvis also called the motion "poisonous antisemitism, a threat to British Jews and to Britain".

The Green Party motion said it "rejects attempts" to - among other things - "equate anti-Zionism with antisemitism" and said "we affirm that definitions of anti-Jewish discrimination should not equate Jewish identity with Zionist ideology or political practice".

Opposition parties pushed back against the motion.

Labour chairwoman Bridget Phillipson said the vote "crosses a line" and called on Polanski to "make clear that this will not be their position moving forwards".

Shadow home secretary Chris Philp criticised the motion on behalf of the Conservatives, saying it demonstrated the Green Party was "toxic to its core".

Liberal Democrat MP Luke Taylor said the "divisive" motion did not address "the rising threats" of Islamophobia and antisemitism in the UK.

articles.title: Tensions exposed among Greens by 'Zionism is racism' conference vote
articles.summary: What may be troubling for the Greens institutionally is what this episode reveals about some of the dynamics in the party.
articles.body:
It is not exactly typical for a British party conference, let alone that of one of the smaller parties, to elicit international condemnation.

Yet that is the position the Green Party of England and Wales is in today after Israel's foreign ministry said it was banning their leader, Zack Polanski, from entering the country.

The cause was the motion proposed by party members and adopted by the conference on Sunday, declaring Zionism, which is the belief in the right to a Jewish homeland, to be racism.

The Green motion describes Zionism as an ideology supporting "an ethnonationalist Jewish state", and supports instead a "single democratic Palestinian state in all of historic Palestine".

It's hardly likely that Polanski or indeed many Greens are going to be much troubled by Israel's condemnation of the motion. One major factor in the Greens' electoral gains over the past year or so, a hugely successful period for the party, has been their clear and vocal condemnation of Israel's war in Gaza and actions in the region more generally.

What may be more troubling for the Greens institutionally is what this episode reveals about some of the dynamics in the party.

Many Greens are proud of the party's internal democracy: this motion was proposed by and voted on by party members. Yet that has resulted in the scenario of leading Green elected politicians facing scrutiny over party policy which the vast majority of them opposed.

Polanski, who is not an MP, wanted changes to the motion which were rejected by the conference, and ultimately did not participate in the debate or vote. Of the Greens' five MPs, four opposed the motion.

The most vocal of them was Adrian Ramsay, the MP for Waveney Valley, who was a Green co-leader for four years until September last year when he and his running mate were defeated by Polanski by a vast margin.

Polanski banned from Israel after party's motion declaring 'Zionism is racism'

Jewish Greens chair says she could leave party over 'Zionism is racism' motion

So an element of this is the changing nature of the Greens' activist base under Polanski's leadership, moving away from an environmental focus to a more general left-populist politics, incorporating a large element of 'anti-imperialist' foreign policy.

Yet this may not be the last issue where that results in a public dispute between the membership and their MPs, four of whom were elected at the last general election under different leadership.

And it is striking that, though Polanski's election as leader was a clear symbol of that shift in the Greens' approach, he did not back this motion. So this could presage tensions too between Polanski and the party membership, some of whom will have been inspired to join the Greens by his leadership.

In practical terms, the Green MPs will be able to continue espousing a different position in parliament to the party's new policy.

The Greens do not have a whipping system, meaning that MPs are free to vote as they wish. This is also true of their councillors, including in the almost 40 councils where the Greens are in power after the May local elections.

It will be interesting to see whether as a result of these tensions there is a push either to constrain the ability of the party conference to make policy, or in the other direction - to constrain the ability of elected representatives to defy party policy.

Separately, this motion may present a political headache down the line for Andy Burnham.

In his Labour conference speech last week, the prime minister said he was forming a "national commission" on electoral reform, with a view to changing the system used for general elections in the long-term.

While Burnham did not specify what system he wanted, he said that Labour would at the next general election commit to a new system where "everyone's vote counts and everyone's voice is heard".

Under a move to any more proportional system, on current trends, there would likely be more Green MPs as a result. In the scenario of a hung parliament, the Greens are a party to which Labour would naturally look for support as part of the progressive bloc.

And yet the Greens are also now a party whose actions this weekend have been condemned by the Labour chair, Bridget Phillipson, as "shameful" and "fundamentally wrong". Angela Rayner, the communities secretary, said the Zionism motion "crosses a line and is rightly being condemned across the political spectrum."

Labour has long been divided on the question of electoral reform. Their leader now has a clear position in favour but the Green motion this weekend could have the unintended effect of bolstering opposition within Labour to that element of the prime minister's agenda.

Robert MacIntyre may have played his final event of the season because of ongoing uncertainty over the situation in the Middle East.

Scotland's top golfer finished tied for sixth at the Alfred Dunhill Links Championship at St Andrews on Sunday, having won the title 12 months ago.

The 30-year-old will not play in this week's Spanish Open and currently has no plans to compete in India or South Korea before the DP World Tour's season-ending events in Abu Dhabi and Dubai in November.

MacIntyre says he will wait to see how conflicts in the Middle East develop before deciding whether to play in either event.

Fellow Ryder Cup player Matt Fitzpatrick has also expressed doubts about travelling to the region, but world number two Rory McIlroy has confirmed he intends to play in both events.

"This is potentially the end of my season right here," MacIntyre told BBC Scotland after his final round at the Dunhill Links.

"I feel like it's been a good year. It's been a learning curve, trying to manage life outside of golf and life on the golf course. It's been a great year.

"I don't even know when the cut-off is. It'll probably be the week before it. I'll literally sit and wait and see what's going on in the Middle East. Then I'll make a decision.

"If I'm in the tournament, I'm in the tournament. Then I'll make a decision."

Scott into top 100 after second Korn Ferry Tour win

Stewart up 496 places after fourth at Alfred Dunhill Links

MacIntyre said he could still play in the Bahamas in December, but that decision would depend on how his preparations for next season progress.

"Right now, before I was playing today, I'll probably play in the Bahamas in December, see how my work's been getting on," he said. "We'll make a decision on that at the end of the time.

"It's going to be a quiet two-and-a-bit months, I think.

"Try and lose a bit of weight. Get in the gym. Do a bit to the house. Hopefully build a simulator at the house. Life's good."

Whatever decision he makes, MacIntyre will return to St Andrews next summer when the Old Course hosts the 155th Open Championship.

The world number 19's top-six finish this week suggests he is finally beginning to appreciate the demands of the famous course.

The Old Course has undergone a number of changes in recent years, including new bunkers and tees on some holes.

"I love the town - I've always said that," MacIntyre said. "We come here on family holidays. St Andrews is a special, special place.

"The golf course was never my favourite, but it's starting to grow on me. A lot of people have said that, the more you play it, the more you start to enjoy it.

"Obviously, the success has helped that. I'm starting to see things where I can push a little bit more up off the tee shots on certain holes or other holes.

articles.title: Mexico seeks evidence of border shooting that prompted US troop deployment
articles.summary: Mexico’s Sheinbaum has expressed concern about US officials overstepping norms on security cooperation.
articles.body:
Mexico has asked the United States for evidence of a cross-border shooting that allegedly targeted US security personnel.

In her daily news conference on Monday, Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum explained that the US had reported “shots from the Mexican border”.

“We asked for all the evidence because we have no evidence,” Sheinbaum said. She added that Mexico’s National Guard, Army and Navy had not detected any shots being fired from Mexican territory towards the US.

Sheinbaum made her remarks a day after the US Ambassador to Mexico Ronald Johnson wrote on the social media platform X about the shooting, which allegedly took place in Texas across from the Mexican state of Tamaulipas in late September.

Johnson said the targets were members of the US Coast Guard, and that the threat would be “swiftly addressed”.

“The U.S. Embassy in Mexico is helping coordinate with Mexican forces deploying to the border area where U.S. Coast Guardsmen were fired upon,” Johnson wrote.

“Together, we intend to patrol both sides of our shared border, protect our communities, and make it more difficult for criminal and terrorist organizations to operate.”

Some 500 US troops, along with helicopters, drones and anti-drone equipment, have been sent to the border since the alleged shooting.

Mexico has sent its own deployment in the border area, as part of a joint operation called Operation Mirror between the two countries to secure the frontier.

In Monday’s news conference, Sheinbaum confirmed that the Mexican deployment was designed “to forestall any issues” that may arise.

During their time working together, Johnson and Sheinbaum have repeatedly been at odds over questions of border security and national sovereignty.

A former US Army Green Beret who later served in the Central Intelligence Agency (CIA), Johnson has served as ambassador to Mexico since May 2025, under US President Donald Trump.

Since returning to office for a second term, Trump has sought to increase US influence over Latin America, as part of a policy informally dubbed the Donroe Doctrine — a twist on the 19th-century Monroe Doctrine.

His administration has also taken a more active role in the region’s security, on the premise of combatting narcotics trafficking and criminal organisations.

Trump has repeatedly said he may carry out military strikes inside Mexico to attack the cartels he said are “running Mexico”, framing their presence as a threat to US security. Sheinbaum, however, has warned that such an operation would violate her country’s sovereignty.

Mexico’s tensions with the Trump administration have strained relations with Johnson. Sheinbaum has accused the ambassador of overstepping diplomatic norms, while Johnson has sought to push the Mexican government to cooperate with Trump’s demands.

In June, Johnson criticised Sheinbaum’s government on social media for turning the “fight against cartels” into a “political dispute”.

Sheinbaum responded the next day with a warning for Johnson, saying, “Ambassadors must respect the internal political affairs of their countries.”

Law enforcement agencies in the US and Mexico have long cooperated in counter-narcotics operations, but Trump’s militaristic approach has created friction with left-wing governments including Mexico.

On Monday, Sheinbaum took issue with Johnson for announcing the opening of an international police academy in the central state of Queretaro without her government’s knowledge.

“How can a groundbreaking ceremony take place with a US ambassador and a Mexican governor, but not with the federal security cabinet?” she said.

Under the Mexican constitution, the federal government must approve the activities of foreign forces on Mexican soil.

But that law was tested earlier this year, when two CIA agents were reportedly killed in an April car accident in the northern Mexican state of Chihuahua, alongside members of the state’s law enforcement.

What the CIA agents were doing in Chihuahua remains unclear. Reports emerged that the CIA agents may have been participating in a state-led raid on a local drug lab without federal authorisation.

One state official publicly denied that report, saying the agents were conducting an unrelated training on drone usage.

Sheinbaum said neither she nor her cabinet were informed of any CIA activities, and her government pledged to investigate the incident.

articles.title: I won't accept exclusion, says Polanski after backlash to Zionist motion
articles.summary: Labour MPs and the European Greens have demanded clarity from the Green Party over a "Zionism is racism" motion.
articles.body:
Zack Polanski has said he will not accept anyone being excluded from the Green Party "because of the religious or communal body they are part of", after members adopted a motion declaring Zionism a form of racism.

The Green leader said "no-one will be made unwelcome because of their background, their faith, or where they worship".

The motion defines Zionism as an ideology supporting "an ethnonationalist Jewish state" and backs a "single democratic Palestinian state in all of historic Palestine".

It comes after more than a dozen Labour MPs reported the Greens to the equality watchdog on Monday, saying it raised "serious questions".

Tensions exposed among Greens by 'Zionism is racism' conference vote

Nine Labour MPs have also referred the Green Party to Sussex Police, asking the force to investigate whether alleged "possible antisemitic offences" at the conference merit a criminal investigation.

Sussex Police and the Green Party have been contacted for comment.

It is the latest development in a backlash to the policy motion , which was put forward by a group of activists at the party's conference in Brighton and endorsed by 1,022 votes to 813.

"The real, material, manifestation of Zionism has been the historic and ongoing dehumanisation, displacement, dispossession, disenfranchisement and destruction of Palestinians," it said.

The motion has exposed divisions between the party's newly enlarged membership base under leader Zack Polanski and its MPs elected at the last general election.

Polanski did not take part in the vote on Sunday and four of the party's five MPs opposed it.

Israel's foreign ministry responded by banning Polanski from entering the country, while some Jewish groups have described it as an "attack on the Jewish community".

In his first comments since the motion was passed, having declined interviews on Monday, Polanski released a lengthy statement saying he "take[s] seriously my responsibility to make sure everyone feels safe and welcome in our party".

He added: "As leader I will not accept any exclusion, or refusal to engage with anyone, because of the religious or communal body they are part of."

He said his party and its leadership stood for "deeply held values of compassion, fairness and equality for all".

Polanski, who is Jewish, added that "antisemitism and criticism of the Israeli state are, and must always be, completely distinct".

On Monday, a group of Labour MPs wrote two letters to the Equality and Human Rights Commission (EHRC) - organised by former Home Office minister Mike Tapp - raising concerns about the motion, and amendments to protect Jewish members attending Zionist synagogues being voted down.

"Taken together, these developments raise serious questions about whether Jewish members can participate freely and equally in the party, and whether their religious and communal connections could expose them to complaints or disciplinary action," their letter to the watchdog said.

The EHRC, which regulates equality law in Great Britain, previously found failings in how Labour handled antisemitism.

In a statement following the letter, the EHRC told the BBC it would "consider each complaint carefully" and had not at this stage launched an investigation.

It added: "We have guidance advising political parties on their responsibilities under the Equality Act 2010. Like all duty-bearers, political parties must comply with the Act and take steps to avoid discrimination."

The European Green Party, of which the Green Party for England and Wales is a member, released a statement on Monday saying it wanted to "unequivocally distance" itself from the motion.

The umbrella body said it would "immediately demand clarity" from the party's leadership on how they would protect Jewish people and self-determination.

Meanwhile, Green MP Ellie Chowns told Radio 4's PM programme she was "deeply saddened" the motion had become party policy but disagreed it was antisemitic, saying it was underpinned by "principled opposition to the actions of the Israeli government".

She suggested a review of Green policymaking processes was needed since "less than 1%" of the party's more than 200,000 members had participated in the vote.

articles.title: West Allegheny's Nico Ward continues impressive year with WPIAL title
articles.summary: West Allegheny golfer Nico Ward has been on an incredible run the past six months. That run continued at the WPIAL 3A championships with a title.
articles.body:
BELL ACRES — Throughout the past six months, West Allegheny High School boys golfer Nico Ward has been on an incredible run.

From being one step away from qualifying for the 2026 U.S. Open to tying a course record during the high school golf season, Ward has had a year to remember for someone who is only a junior in high school.

At the WPIAL 3A boys high school golf championships on Monday, Oct. 5 at Sewickley Heights Golf Club, Ward's impressive year continued, capturing gold for the first time in his career.

"I just hung in there all day, didn't make many mistakes and played bogey-free golf," Ward said. "I knew that if I could continue to apply pressure throughout the round, everything would work out."

See the best shots from the WPIAL high school golf championships

The win for Ward marks just the third individual champion to come from West Allegheny, joining Harry Hamilton (1968) and Mike Phillips (1970-71).

Coming into the final round four shots off the lead, the junior needed just two birdies to win the title, finishing by carding a 70 (-2).

"I knew that I had to come out today, play solid and not make any stupid mistakes," Ward said. "I was hitting fairways and greens pretty much all day and giving myself birdie looks, so I am proud of myself for that."

As Ward wrapped up his WPIAL individual season and now sets his sights on the PIAA golf championships, he has had one of the more unique runs that a high school golfer could have.

Back in the spring, Ward's year began at the U.S. Open qualifying on May 12 at Weymouth Country Club in Medina, OH, surviving a five-hole playoff and finishing birdie-birdie to card a 69.

With that score, the junior went on to play on golf's longest day, finishing +5 at Springfield Country Club in June.

Ward pulled back on his experience playing alongside some of the world's best golfers as he was competing for gold in the WPIAL's final round to help him capture gold.

"The U.S. Open pins were unreal. Some were in some diabolical spots, so to come out here and face some dicey pin locations, it wasn't so bad compared to what I was used to playing," Ward said.

The momentum that Ward gained from participating in U.S. Open qualifying carried into the high school season as he and his West Allegheny teammates rolled through section play.

With Ward leading the way as the team's top golfer in the lineup, West Allegheny captured its first section title since 2010, posting an 11-1 mark, with its lone section loss coming against Moon Area.

The trio of golfers consisting of Ward, fellow junior Levi Vaughn and sophomore Ethan Bobonski have all had impressive seasons, with the trio qualifying for the WPIAL championships, with Ward (-1), Bobonski (+12) and Vaughn (+12) all qualifying for states.

"We've got a great group of guys out there this year," Ward said. "I couldn't ask for much more; I hope we can make it to the WPIAL and PIAA team championships."

Along with helping the team capture its first title in 16 years, Ward has also had his fair share of individual success, most notably in the lead-up to postseason play.

At the MAC Championships, Ward helped the West Allegheny team capture its third straight title in the event, finishing with a total score of 207 to edge out both Blackhawk and Mars.

The impressive score was spearheaded by Ward, who tied Fox Run's course record, posting a 64 (-8).

"I had no idea what the course record was there until I looked on their website late in the round," Ward said. "It was a great experience, birding the last hole to tie the record."

Now, Ward will be competing at the PIAA golf championships at Penn State's White Course on Monday, Oct. 19.

After finishing sixth overall as a sophomore, Ward will be aiming to add one more accolade to his resume as his high school golf season comes to a close.

"I couldn't ask for a better junior career than this," Ward said. "I hope that I can continue to keep all this success rolling."

articles.title: The bizarre rule Paul Casey was questioned about on his way to winning the 2019 European Open
articles.summary: One of the strangest rules violations very nearly took place during the second round of the 2019 Porsche European Open when Paul Casey holed an eight-foot pu...
articles.body:
One of the strangest rules violations very nearly took place during the second round of the 2019 Porsche European Open when Paul Casey holed an eight-foot putt.

Casey secured his 14th victory on the European Tour that week in Germany. The Englishman finished one shot clear of a handful of players, including Robert MacIntyre.

However, one putt during the second round could have landed him in some bother after replays had shown that his ball had rolled over a bug on the green.

Casey was completely unaware that the bug had been on his line. It turns out if he had known it was there and hit it, he would have been forced to re-hit the putt as it is considered an animal.

How Paul Casey reacted to strange incident at the 2019 Porsche European Open

It was while the five-time Ryder Cup star was in scoring after his round of 73 that he was informed of the potential violation. However, Casey was cleared of any wrongdoing once he confirmed that he did not realise that the bug had been on his line and was hit by his ball.

He went on to speak to the media about the bizarre incident.

"I putted the ball, when I looked up the ball was going at the hole, just crept in left edge," he said.

"And he's [the rules official] just showed me the video, it actually ran straight over the poor bug, hopefully I didn't hurt him.

"If you knowingly hit an animal, and a bug is considered an animal, during the course of a stroke certainly on the putting green, you have to replay it.

"I didn't knowingly hit it, so I'm alright but yeah almost a rules infraction and I had no clue."

What Casey would not have realised at the time was how costly the incident could have been had the circumstances been ever so slightly different.

Casey went into the final round at Winsen one shot adrift of the lead. However, a flawless round of 66 on Sunday saw him win the title.

It was actually his first win on the European Tour in nearly five years.

Given that Casey is one of those exceptionally talented players without a major victory during his career, the 2019 Porsche European Open may well go down as one of the more memorable wins he has had simply due to the events of that second round.

Romeo Doubs just delivered the kind of fantasy football performance that can make managers feel untouchable. That said, ESPN insider Dan Graziano believes it may actually be the perfect time to sell. After the New England Patriots ' thrilling 29-26 road victory over the Buffalo Bills, Doubs emerged as Drake Maye's favorite boundary target . However, his Week 4 breakout may not be sustainable once the Patriots' receiving corps gets healthier.

Doubs caught six of nine targets for 58 yards and two touchdowns. He produced a valuable fantasy football outing in a nationally significant Patriots win. Graziano, however, urged managers to capitalize immediately .

"Sell Romeo Doubs this week if you have him. NOT AN OVERREACTION."

He pointed to Doubs' modest yardage total, his inconsistent production earlier this season, and the eventual return of AJ Brown as reasons to move him while his fantasy football value is elevated.

Brown's absence has created additional opportunities for Doubs, particularly around the red zone. Once Brown returns from his ankle injury, however, Maye's target distribution could shift significantly. That could push Doubs back into a secondary role within an offense that can also lean on its rushing attack and tight end Hunter Henry.

Doubs entered the NFL after Green Bay selected him in the fourth round of the 2022 draft out of Nevada. Across four seasons with the Packers, he recorded more than 200 receptions, nearly 2,500 yards, and 21 touchdowns before signing with New England in 2026. His reliable hands and red-zone ability have quickly made him a trusted option for Maye.

For fantasy football managers, the message is simple: Doubs' Week 4 explosion may be the peak of his current market value. Graziano believes the time to cash in is now.

articles.summary: El jugador espera estos días el nacimiento de su cuarto hijo, que aún no se ha producido, y se ha visto obligado a renunciar al torneo
articles.body: Jon Rahm no participará en el Open de España by Madrid, torneo que comienza este próximo jueves en el Club de Campo de la capital de España. Será la primera vez que el golfista de Barrika se ausenta del gran torneo español, que ha ganado en tres ocasiones (2018, 19 y 22), desde que debutó exitosamente aquel año. El jugador espera estos días el nacimiento de su cuarto hijo, que aún no se ha producido, y se ha visto obligado a renunciar a este evento madrileño. El torneo, no obstante, contará con un plantel de golfistas de primer nivel con cuatro ganadores del Masters de Augusta (Patrick Reed, Bubba Watson, Danny Willet y Sergio García), dos vencedores del British (Shane Lowry y Francesco Molinari), un campeón del US Open (Justin Rose), además de otros jugadores de indiscutible valor como David Puig, Eugenio López-Chacarra, Ángel Ayora, Josele Ballester, Ludvig Aberg, Tyrrell Hatton y el defensor del título Marco Penge.

articles.title: Deadline for LIV golfers to commit league's future pushed back as initial $300 million in funding put in place
articles.summary: BC Partners' $300 million investment extends the LIV Golf commitment deadline as players like Bryson DeChambeau and Jon Rahm weigh their futures.
articles.body: Players sitting on the fence contemplating whether or not to commit to LIV Golf's future will be allowed to sit a bit longer. LIV Golf officially extended the deadline for players to commit to the league, moving the date from Oct. 13 to Oct. 25, on the heels of BC Partners making its initial investment in "LIV 2.0" with a target of $300 million to bring the circuit out of Chapter 11 bankruptcy. LIV Golf filed for bankruptcy in September after the Saudi Public Investment Fund – the sole funder of the league since its inception in 2022 – made the decision to withdraw all financial support at the end of the 2026 season. The Saudis had spent $5 billion to fund the league before shutting off the financial spigot. RORY MCILROY GETS SNARKY ON THE RETURN OF LIV GOLF PLAYERS TO PGA TOUR: 'HAVE THEY BROUGHT VALUE?' While the future of LIV Golf remains up in the air, BC Partners making its financial commitment two days before hearings related to the league's bankruptcy filing begin can only be considered a step in the right direction. The financial commitment and funding from BC Partners now require bankruptcy approval, and if it is achieved, LIV would then move forward with building out a 2027 season, which would include a 10-tournament schedule with half of the events taking place internationally. THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW! We want the players who make this league what it is to share in what they help build," Ted Goldthorpe, partner and head of BC Partners Credit, said in a statement. "Giving players real and actionable ownership in the league and the teams is a unique opportunity in professional golf, and it aligns everyone around the long-term success of the product for the game and for the fans." It was announced in August that players competing on the next iteration of LIV Golf would hold a majority of equity, with LIV CEO Scott O'Neil explaining the league will be "driven by and for the players." SIGN UP FOR THE DAILY OUTKICK NEWSLETTER The most notable players still associated with LIV Golf include Bryson DeChambeau, Jon Rahm, Joaquin Niemann, Cameron Smith, and Tyrrell Hatton. It is understood that, given LIV's bankruptcy and restructuring, players could be released from any existing contracts with the circuit, meaning they could then look at other opportunities. At the moment, the PGA Tour is not providing any sort of straightforward path for players who previously defected to LIV.
